source.title: Beyond Performance Plateaus: A Comprehensive Study on Scalability in Speech Enhancement
source.authors: Wang-You Zhang; Kohei Saijo; Jee-weon Jung; Chen-Da Li; Shinji Watanabe; Yan-Min Qian

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps model complexity and evaluates held-out performance, and explicitly reports a double-descent-like result. It uses speech-enhancement metrics and does not locate an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-complexity trends for BSRNN and data-scale trends. Its discussion of the small-data result is explicit; plotted values themselves are not stated in the text. It does not report epoch-wise curves or test error at an identified interpolation threshold.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps BSRNN model complexity in speech enhancement, a new setting, and reports held-out quality that degrades then improves on the 9 h corpus. The authors explicitly call this double descent, which bears on V1. It is T3 rather than T2 because the method is a standard size sweep and only the domain and metrics are new.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors call the 9 h complexity trend double descent and conclude that small corpora such as VCTK+DEMAND are unsuitable for benchmarking high-capacity SE models. They also call for large, balanced, multi-domain corpora and more efficiently scalable architectures, since RNN-based models scale inefficiently.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps trained model complexity and evaluates speech-enhancement quality on test corpora, but does not measure test error against training fit or locate an interpolation threshold.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported complexity trend differs by training-data scale and metric: the initial degradation followed by improvement is reported for SDR, PESQ-WB, and STOI on 9 h; the authors say increasing complexity generally improves metrics when sufficient data are available.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing data from 157 h to about 900 h by adding simulated DNS-2020 data degraded overall performance. The authors attribute this to a highly imbalanced, mismatched data distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding more data from a dominant, mismatched source can reduce speech-enhancement performance.

record.problems: The text does not give numerical values or uncertainty estimates for the relevant plotted trends. The double-descent interpretation is limited to a small-data condition and is not tied to a measured interpolation threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant results were omitted.

untested.parts: No training-fit measure, so the peak is not located at the interpolation threshold. The first descent before the peak is not reported: degradation starts from the smallest model. Values appear only in figures.
Data scaling (9/99/157 h) is not examined near an interpolation threshold. Only monotonic gains are reported (r7, r8).
Only deep SE architectures; no non-deep model classes and no located interpolation points.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location. The #MACs vs #Params comparison concerns cross-architecture correlation, not peak location.
No label-noise, regularization or multiple-peak experiments.
Complexity is not re-expressed as an effective parameter count to test whether the second descent disappears.

missing.what: Model-complexity sweeps at 99 h and 157 h show general improvement with complexity and no degradation phase, which bears on where V1's peak appears.
missing.locator: Section 3.1, Fig. 1, first and second bullets

missing.what: At 9 h the exception is stated only for SDR, PESQ-WB and STOI. DNSMOS and WAcc are not reported as showing the degradation.
Authors place over-capacity above about 10 G/s MACs for 9 h of data, an informal threshold location.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3 because speech enhancement is a new setting for a standard size sweep. All V1 evidence is figure-only, averaged over matched and mismatched test sets. The double-descent interpretation rests on the authors' wording, with no training-error or interpolation measurement.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not identify the size at which the training set is just fit, and reports enhancement quality metrics rather than test error.
No epoch-wise performance curve is reported.
The data-scale experiments do not identify or test a condition near an interpolation threshold.
The architecture comparison does not test a general double-descent curve across model classes or locate their interpolation points.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
The study does not test label-noise or regularization effects, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not re-express complexity as an effective number of parameters or test whether that removes the second descent.

relationships.reason: Text reports only initial degradation then improvement (r1-r6). The curve is a rise-then-fall without a shown first descent or a located threshold, it is figure-only, and it is limited to some metrics.

source_check.condition: Causal and non-causal BSRNN trained on 9 h (VCTK+DEMAND), SDR/PESQ-WB/STOI averaged over all test sets
source_check.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly reports degradation followed by recovery for r1–r6, an incomplete V1 pattern. Training interpolation and the preceding error descent are not established. These intrusive metrics use simulated test samples only.

relationships.condition: BSRNN trained on 99 h and 157 h
relationships.reason: Per the text, not the rows: complexity 'generally improves all metrics' with more data, so no rise is reported. The pattern appears only at the smallest data scale within the tested size range.
relationships.display_finding: With 99 h and 157 h of training data, increasing model complexity generally improved all metrics without a reported degradation.
